messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 40
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Surgeon
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 49

He is 40, a Latin American man who has built his life around precision, calm hands, and the expectation that emergencies can be managed if one stays focused enough. Before the disaster, his days as a surgeon are long but structured. He moves between the operating room, rounds, family dinners, and the ordinary routines of a married life that has, until recently, felt stable. He is proud of how dependable he is. People trust him. He trusts systems, timing, and preparation.

That sense of order changes the day the natural disaster strikes. He is at work when the ground begins to move and the building lurches with a force he cannot anticipate or control. At first he thinks it will pass quickly, something he can outlast by staying still and thinking clearly. Instead, the shaking intensifies. Lights fail. Alarms sound. He hears metal snapping somewhere in the building, the crush of objects falling, people shouting in voices that do not sound like their own. In the chaos he is acutely aware of his own body—his heart hammering, his hands suddenly clumsy, his breathing shallow and fast. He tries to help others, tries to become the person everyone can look to, but the scale of the destruction makes that role feel fragile and temporary. The hospital, the place where he is accustomed to being in charge, becomes unsafe in an instant.

In the hours and days after, he moves through the disaster zone on autopilot. He helps with injuries, improvises care, searches for colleagues, and checks repeatedly on his family. Even when he is physically safe, he feels as if he is still waiting for the next violent movement. He does not sleep well. When he does drift off, he wakes abruptly to imagined shaking, his body already braced. He begins to notice how often he scans his surroundings: the ceiling, the exit routes, the stability of the walls, the sounds from outside. He avoids being on the upper floors of buildings when he can, and he becomes tense in elevators, at the first rumble of construction, with sirens, even with the low vibration of a passing truck. His wife notices that he pauses before entering rooms, as if measuring them for danger.

As time passes, the memories do not settle into the past. They arrive without warning while he is scrubbing in, reviewing scans, or sitting at the table at home. A certain smell of dust, antiseptic mixed with debris, can bring him back to the moment the lights went out. The sound of metal trays clattering in the operating room can make his stomach drop. He does not describe these experiences easily, but in session he says that the images come “like a flash,” and for a few seconds he is back in the building, feeling the ground move beneath him. He works harder to keep control, throwing himself into long shifts and extra tasks, but he also finds that concentration slips. He rereads charts. He second-guesses decisions that used to feel automatic. The effort of appearing steady takes more energy than he wants to admit.

At home, he is more irritable than before. Small disruptions—someone interrupting him, a door left open, a plan changing suddenly—can trigger a sharpness in his tone that surprises even him. He feels guilty afterward and tries to repair the moment quickly, especially with his wife, who has become used to reading the tension in his face before he speaks. He loves his family deeply, and that love now sits beside a constant undercurrent of dread. He checks on them more than he used to, texts when he should be resting, and feels an almost physical relief only when everyone is accounted for.

He has also become less able to enjoy the parts of life that used to ground him. Meals are quieter. Weekends feel less restorative. He no longer relaxes in the easy way his wife remembers, and he notices that he has grown distant from friends. There is a heaviness in him that he finds difficult to name. He is not simply sad; he feels changed, as if the disaster has altered his nervous system and his view of the world at the same time. He still functions, still performs surgery, still shows up, but he does so with a vigilance that never fully turns off. The man who once believed that skill and preparation could keep danger at bay now lives with the knowledge that catastrophe can arrive without warning and leave its imprint in the body long after the ground has stopped moving.
